newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl laments German unemployed rejecting jobs.
newsitem.headline: Kohl laments German unemployed rejecting jobs.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Thursday it was "absurd" German employers were having to take on foreign workers at a time of record unemployment but he warned politicians not to inflame ethnic tensions over the issue.

Speaking one day after his conservative coalition partners in the Christian Social Union (CSU) called for stricter limits on foreigners as part of a plan to cut unemployment, Kohl told journalists the current system clearly needed to be changed.

"It is rather absurd that we have a job market in Germany with many areas where jobs are being offered but not accepted," said Kohl, whose Christian Democratic Union rules together with the CSU and the liberal Free Democrats.

"This situation can certainly not remain the way it is," the chancellor added, but admitted he had not yet made up his mind about how to change it. "This has nothing to do with ideology or xenophobia."

With unemployment climbing to a postwar record high of 10.3 percent in December, Kohl said he could understand how wage earners were frustrated by unemployed Germans turning down jobs which ended up being filled by foreign workers.
"The average wage earner just cannot understand having taxes and employment insurance deducted while at the same time we have a situation like we have here," Kohl said.
Kohl said just a few hundred metres away from his private home in Oggersheim there were vegetable farmers who could not find Germans willing to work in the fields.
The same, he said, is true at construction sites in front of the Reichstag building in Berlin.

"Go there and ask the foreman to tell you the truth about how many workers are German citizens," Kohl said. "Then go to the Berlin unemployment office and find out how many unemployed construction workers there are."
Kohl said, however, that politicians needed to use extreme care when discussing the issue.

"The democratic parties need to be very careful that this subject isn't used in a certain direction in upcoming elections," he said, a remark that followed CSU proposals to prohibit non-European Union foreigners from obtaining work permits in Germany for five years.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, chairman of the CSU, said on Wednesday it was "grotesque" that millions of Germans were unemployed while so many foreigners were working here.

CSU parliamentary leader Michael Glos said the party's aim was to stop the immigration of foreigners from outside the European Union. Four million Germans are jobless while more than one million foreigners receive work permits each year, he said.
The CSU, the most right-wing of Germany's mainstream parties and a junior partner in Kohl's ruling coalition, has long been noted for its arch-conservative views.

But the Bavarian party and other mainstream political forces have long refrained from directly linking the high unemployment level to the eight million foreign residents, in part because they want to avoid being accused of fomenting racial unrest.
They have been especially careful since xenophobic violence erupted in Germany in the early 1990s.
